description: MemoOS is a science and software team joining NASA Space Apps 2026. I’m a cybersecurity master’s student and developer with experience in Python, web development, data analysis, and scientific visualization. Our goal is to make SPHEREx sky data accessible through an interactive web tool. We’re looking for teammates interested in astrophysics, astronomy data, UI/UX, and scientific storytelling. Spanish and English speakers are welcome!
summary:
SPHEREx Sky Explorer is an interactive web application for exploring repeated NASA SPHEREx observations at five official challenge targets: Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855−0714, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis. Visitors can select an object, enter custom sky coordinates (RA/Dec), and compare two real infrared exposures with a blink animation and image slider.

Our reproducible Python/Astropy pipeline searches NASA/IPAC-IRSA Level 2 FITS data, checks sky-position alignment, effective wavelength, and pixel-quality flags, and publishes traceable datasets for the browser. All five target fields have two-epoch views. Three pass preliminary quality checks at the predicted object position. In Barnard’s Star and R Draconis, the central positions are masked, so their views honestly compare the surrounding field and also offer single exposures.

The tool makes archival astronomy more accessible without claiming a discovery: the previews do not establish actual motion or variability. The public app and source code are available for anyone to explore.
details:
Overview

SPHEREx Sky Explorer is an independent, browser-based scientific visualization prototype designed to make repeated SPHEREx observations easier to explore and understand.

Our goal is to demonstrate the foundations of comparing the same region of sky across observing epochs, a necessary step when investigating changes or possible moving astronomical sources.

Scientific workflow

We accessed real NASA SPHEREx Level 2 data from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA).

Our Python pipeline queried the DR1 and QR3 collections using the SIA2 service. For a selected sky coordinate, we retrieved metadata for 443 image records: 330 from DR1 and 113 from QR3.

We examined FITS cutouts using Astropy, evaluated spatial World Coordinate System (WCS) information, inspected quality flags, and estimated the effective wavelengths of candidate observations.

For our selected demonstration pair, observations from 2025 and 2026 share 121 of 144 sampled sky positions. Of these, 118 samples passed our preliminary quality criteria in the visualization. The approximate difference between the effective central wavelengths is 8.68 nm.

The processed image arrays were exported as JSON for use in the web application.

User experience

The public Next.js application allows visitors to:

  • View two real SPHEREx observations.
  • Switch between the 2025 and 2026 epochs.
  • Use an animated blink or slider to compare images.
  • Inspect observing metadata and preliminary quality metrics.
  • Access the original NASA data and the open-source code.

Technology

The project uses Python, NumPy, Astropy, FITS, WCS, TypeScript, Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, GitHub, and Vercel.

Scientific integrity and future impact

This is an exploratory demonstration of one small sky field, not an automated discovery system. Different effective wavelengths and possible instrumental or calibration effects prevent us from interpreting visible brightness differences as confirmed astronomical variability.

Future development could expand the analysis to additional fields and spectral bands, improve spectral and photometric calibration, and introduce validated methods for identifying candidate moving or variable objects.
